transcript: In this segment we study linear regression. Fit a line or hyperplane that predicts a continuous target from features.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study linear regression. Fit a line or hyperplane that predicts a continuous target from features.

ocr_text: Linear Regression. Linear Regression. Fit a line or hyperplane that predicts a continuous target from features. Formula: \hat{y} = x^\top \theta. A scatter plot with a fitted prediction line.

formula_blocks.latex: \hat{y} = x^\top \theta

visual_caption: A scatter plot with a fitted prediction line.

transcript: In this segment we study mean squared error. The loss function averages squared prediction errors over examples.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study mean squared error. The loss function averages squared prediction errors over examples.

ocr_text: Linear Regression. Mean Squared Error. The loss function averages squared prediction errors over examples. Formula: J(\theta)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_i(\hat{y}_i-y_i)^2. Residual arrows from points to the regression line.

formula_blocks.latex: J(\theta)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_i(\hat{y}_i-y_i)^2

visual_caption: Residual arrows from points to the regression line.

transcript: In this segment we study normal equation. For full-rank linear regression, the closed-form optimum solves the least-squares objective.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study normal equation. For full-rank linear regression, the closed-form optimum solves the least-squares objective.

ocr_text: Linear Regression. Normal Equation. For full-rank linear regression, the closed-form optimum solves the least-squares objective. Formula: \theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y. A matrix equation links X, y, and theta.

formula_blocks.latex: \theta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y

visual_caption: A matrix equation links X, y, and theta.

transcript: In this segment we study bias and variance. Simple models may underfit while overly flexible models may overfit training data.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study bias and variance. Simple models may underfit while overly flexible models may overfit training data.

ocr_text: Linear Regression. Bias and Variance. Simple models may underfit while overly flexible models may overfit training data. Formula: \mathrm{error}=bias^2+variance+\sigma^2. Three curves compare underfit, good fit, and overfit behavior.

formula_blocks.latex: \mathrm{error}=bias^2+variance+\sigma^2

visual_caption: Three curves compare underfit, good fit, and overfit behavior.

transcript: In this segment we study gradient descent. Move parameters opposite to the gradient to reduce the objective.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study gradient descent. Move parameters opposite to the gradient to reduce the objective.

ocr_text: Gradient Descent. Gradient Descent. Move parameters opposite to the gradient to reduce the objective. Formula: \theta := \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta). A point walks downhill on a loss surface.

formula_blocks.latex: \theta := \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)

visual_caption: A point walks downhill on a loss surface.

transcript: In this segment we study learning rate. The learning rate controls step size; too large can diverge and too small converges slowly.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study learning rate. The learning rate controls step size; too large can diverge and too small converges slowly.

ocr_text: Gradient Descent. Learning Rate. The learning rate controls step size; too large can diverge and too small converges slowly. Formula: \alpha > 0. Small and large arrows show different optimization step sizes.

formula_blocks.latex: \alpha > 0

visual_caption: Small and large arrows show different optimization step sizes.

transcript: In this segment we study convex loss. For convex objectives, local minima are global minima.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study convex loss. For convex objectives, local minima are global minima.

ocr_text: Gradient Descent. Convex Loss. For convex objectives, local minima are global minima. Formula: J(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\leq \lambda J(a)+(1-\lambda)J(b). A bowl-shaped curve marks the global minimum.

formula_blocks.latex: J(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\leq \lambda J(a)+(1-\lambda)J(b)

visual_caption: A bowl-shaped curve marks the global minimum.

transcript: In this segment we study stochastic gradient. Mini-batches estimate the gradient cheaply and add useful noise during training.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study stochastic gradient. Mini-batches estimate the gradient cheaply and add useful noise during training.

ocr_text: Gradient Descent. Stochastic Gradient. Mini-batches estimate the gradient cheaply and add useful noise during training. Formula: g_t \approx \nabla_\theta J_B(\theta). Noisy arrows move toward a minimum.

formula_blocks.latex: g_t \approx \nabla_\theta J_B(\theta)

visual_caption: Noisy arrows move toward a minimum.

transcript: In this segment we study neural network. Layers compose linear maps and nonlinear activation functions to learn representations.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study neural network. Layers compose linear maps and nonlinear activation functions to learn representations.

ocr_text: Neural Networks. Neural Network. Layers compose linear maps and nonlinear activation functions to learn representations. Formula: h=\sigma(Wx+b). Nodes and edges form a small feed-forward network.

formula_blocks.latex: h=\sigma(Wx+b)

visual_caption: Nodes and edges form a small feed-forward network.

transcript: In this segment we study activation function. Nonlinear activations let networks model relationships beyond linear functions.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study activation function. Nonlinear activations let networks model relationships beyond linear functions.

ocr_text: Neural Networks. Activation Function. Nonlinear activations let networks model relationships beyond linear functions. Formula: \mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z). A ReLU graph is flat for negative inputs and linear for positive inputs.

formula_blocks.latex: \mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)

visual_caption: A ReLU graph is flat for negative inputs and linear for positive inputs.

transcript: In this segment we study chain rule. Backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule to compute gradients layer by layer.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study chain rule. Backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule to compute gradients layer by layer.

ocr_text: Neural Networks. Chain Rule. Backpropagation repeatedly applies the chain rule to compute gradients layer by layer. Formula: \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}. A computational graph highlights local derivatives.

ocr_blocks.text: \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}

formula_latex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}

formula_blocks.latex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}

visual_caption: A computational graph highlights local derivatives.

transcript: In this segment we study backpropagation. Backward passes propagate error signals so each weight receives a learning signal.

asr_segments.text: In this segment we study backpropagation. Backward passes propagate error signals so each weight receives a learning signal.

ocr_text: Neural Networks. Backpropagation. Backward passes propagate error signals so each weight receives a learning signal. Formula: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_l}=\delta_l h_{l-1}^\top. Arrows move backward from loss to earlier layers.

formula_blocks.latex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_l}=\delta_l h_{l-1}^\top

visual_caption: Arrows move backward from loss to earlier layers.

Second-order methods (like Newton-Raphson) use the Hessian to refine the search direction for faster convergence. There exist many improvements of GD (momentum, ADAM), e.g., to smartly control the learn rate, to escape saddle points, to mimic second order behavior without computing the Hessian. If the gradient is not computed on the complete data, but instead on small, random batches, this is stochastic gradient descent (SGD). For large-scale problems, this is usually more efficient. © Introduction to Machine Learning – 10 / 10
